text: Your toddler's vocabulary is growing rapidly and they understand far more words than they can say. Talk to them throughout the day to keep building language skills.
Running, though wobbly, often emerges around 18 months. Give your toddler plenty of outdoor time to practice moving at different speeds.
Your toddler is building toward combining words, which typically happens closer to 2 years. For now, single words with gestures like pointing and saying "milk" are great communication.
Pretend play is blossoming. Your toddler may feed a doll, talk on a toy phone, or pretend to cook. Join in and follow their lead.
Your toddler can likely stack 3-4 blocks now. Try building together and see how high you can go before the fun crash.
Temper tantrums are normal and peak between 18 months and 3 years. Your toddler has big feelings but not yet the words to express them.
Your toddler may point to body parts when you name them. Make a game of it during bath time or while getting dressed.
Walking up stairs while holding your hand is a new challenge your toddler may be ready for. Let them lead and go at their pace.
Your toddler may start saying "no" frequently. This is not defiance but a healthy expression of growing independence and self-awareness.
Try simple sorting activities with two colors or shapes. Your toddler is beginning to understand categories and differences.
Your toddler may show interest in other children, though true cooperative play won't develop until later. Parallel play alongside peers is the norm now.
Kicking a ball is a milestone many toddlers reach around 18 months. Start with a large, soft ball on a flat surface.
Your toddler may try to undress themselves, starting with shoes and socks. Encourage this independence even when it takes extra time.
Reading books with simple stories and pointing at familiar objects strengthens your toddler's comprehension and vocabulary.
Your toddler may follow simple instructions like "bring me your shoes" without needing gestures. This shows growing comprehension, which is a key milestone at this stage.
Most toddlers transition to one nap between 14 and 18 months. If your toddler is down to one nap, it typically lasts 1.5-3 hours in the early afternoon.
Your toddler may experience a sleep regression around this age, often linked to language development, separation anxiety, and newfound independence. Stay consistent with your routine.
Your toddler needs about 11-14 hours of total sleep per day, including their nap. Aim for a bedtime that allows enough nighttime hours.
Toddlers at this age may start stalling at bedtime, asking for one more book or one more drink. Set clear, loving limits with your bedtime routine.
If your toddler is climbing out of the crib, ensure the mattress is at the lowest setting. It is safest to keep them in the crib as long as possible.
Offer choices in the bedtime routine to give your toddler a sense of control: "Do you want the blue pajamas or the green ones?"

Night terrors are most common between ages 2 and 5 but can occasionally start earlier. They look frightening but your toddler is not awake and will not remember them. Avoid waking them during an episode.
Keep the gap between the end of nap time and bedtime at least 4-5 hours. A late nap can push bedtime too far and disrupt the whole schedule.
A visual bedtime chart showing each step of the routine can help your toddler understand what comes next and feel more in control.
If your toddler is resisting the crib, resist the urge to switch to a toddler bed too early. Most children are not ready until at least 2.5-3 years.
Separation anxiety at bedtime can resurge around 18 months. A short, predictable goodbye ritual helps your toddler feel safe.
Active outdoor play during the day promotes better nighttime sleep. Aim for at least 60 minutes of physical activity spread throughout the day.
If your toddler wakes early and plays happily in the crib, it is fine to let them have quiet time until a reasonable wake-up hour.
Dropping the nap is not recommended at 18 months. If your toddler skips a nap occasionally, move bedtime earlier that night.
A consistent wake time, even on weekends, helps regulate your toddler's internal clock and makes naps and bedtime more predictable.
Pediatric guidelines recommend weaning off bottles during this stage. If you have not started yet, begin replacing one bottle at a time with a cup.
Picky eating is at its peak. Continue offering a variety of foods without pressure. Your job is to decide what and when; your toddler decides how much.
Your toddler needs about 1,000-1,400 calories per day, but don't count calories. Offer balanced meals and snacks and trust their appetite.
Offer whole milk or fortified plant milk but limit to {{16-24 ounces|475-710 ml}} daily. Too much milk can fill their belly and reduce appetite for solids.
Your toddler may want to eat only one or two favorite foods. Keep offering other options alongside the preferred foods without making it a battle.
Involve your toddler in meal preparation. They can wash vegetables, tear lettuce, or stir ingredients. Kids who help cook are more likely to eat what they make.
Dipping foods can make meals more exciting for toddlers. Try hummus, yogurt, or mashed avocado as healthy dipping options.
Your toddler's growth rate slows significantly in the second year, which means their appetite may decrease. This is completely normal.
Offer iron-rich foods daily: meat, beans, lentils, fortified cereals, and dark leafy greens. Pair with vitamin C-rich foods to boost absorption.
Snack time is a great opportunity for nutrition. Think of snacks as mini-meals with protein, healthy fat, and fiber rather than just crackers.
Let your toddler practice with a fork by stabbing soft foods like banana chunks, cooked pasta, or cheese cubes. Pre-stab a few pieces to get them started.
If your toddler refuses vegetables, try different preparations: roasted, steamed, in a smoothie, or mixed into pasta sauce. Persistence pays off.
Eating at the table together without distractions like TV or tablets helps your toddler focus on eating and learn from watching the family.
Toddlers often eat better at some meals than others. If breakfast is a hit but dinner is not, do not worry. Look at intake across the full week.
Avoid using food as a reward or comfort. Phrases like "eat your veggies and you can have dessert" can create an unhealthy dynamic around food.
Regular well-child visits during this stage include developmental screening, growth checks, and any vaccines that are due. Bring your list of questions.
Your toddler's first molars typically come in between 13 and 19 months, which can cause significant discomfort. Cold washcloths and age-appropriate pain relief can help.
Continue brushing your toddler's teeth twice daily. Let them try first, then you do a thorough follow-up to make sure all surfaces are cleaned.
If your toddler is not yet using any words, discuss this at the 18-month visit. Early speech therapy can make a meaningful difference.
Toddler diarrhea from too much juice or fruit is common. Limit juice to {{4 ounces|120 ml}} or less per day, and offer whole fruit instead.
Bumps, scrapes, and bruises on shins and foreheads are a normal part of toddlerhood. Clean small wounds with soap and water and apply a bandage.
Apply broad-spectrum sunscreen 15 minutes before going outside and reapply every 2 hours. Don't forget ears, feet, and the back of the neck.
If your toddler has frequent tantrums with head banging, this is usually a phase. Talk to your pediatrician if it becomes very frequent or causes injury.
RSV and flu are more common in cooler months. Teach your toddler to cough into their elbow and wash hands frequently.
Check that your toddler's shoes fit properly with a thumb's width of space at the toe. Feet grow rapidly and shoes may need replacing every few months.
Mild bow legs are normal at this age and usually straighten by age 3. Mention any concerns at your next well-child visit.
If your toddler is toe-walking occasionally, it is usually just exploration. Persistent toe-walking after 2 years should be discussed with your pediatrician.
Developmental screening for autism is recommended around this age. Ask your pediatrician about it if it hasn't been done yet. Early identification leads to the best outcomes from intervention.
Iron deficiency is the most common nutritional deficiency in toddlers. If your toddler seems unusually tired or pale, ask your pediatrician about testing.

Pediatric experts recommend limiting screen media other than video chatting for children under 18 months. Focus on real-world interaction, as nothing replaces face-to-face play for learning at this age.
Give your toddler crayons and a large sheet of paper on the floor. Scribbling is evolving into more intentional marks and is a precursor to writing.
Play dough is a wonderful sensory activity at this age. Your toddler can squeeze, poke, roll, and flatten it, building hand strength.
Set up a pretend kitchen or tea party. Pouring, stirring, and serving develop fine motor skills and social imagination.
Go on a nature walk and collect leaves, sticks, and pinecones in a bag. Sorting and examining them later extends the learning.
Simple puzzles with 3-5 large knob pieces help your toddler develop problem-solving skills and spatial awareness.
Dance parties are perfect for this age. Put on music and model different movements like jumping, spinning, and clapping.
Water play with cups, funnels, and sponges is endlessly fascinating. Set up a bin outdoors or use the bathtub with close supervision.
Hide toys around the room and help your toddler find them. This treasure hunt game builds memory and spatial reasoning.
Your toddler may enjoy playing with dolls or stuffed animals, feeding them, putting them to bed, or giving them hugs. This nurturing play builds empathy.
Let your toddler climb at the playground on age-appropriate equipment. Supervised climbing builds confidence, strength, and coordination.
Try drawing simple shapes and see if your toddler tries to copy them. They may not succeed yet, but attempting is the important part.
Offer a toy broom, dustpan, or watering can. Toddlers love imitating household tasks, and it makes them feel like capable contributors.
Sing songs with actions like "Head, Shoulders, Knees, and Toes." Your toddler will start anticipating the movements and joining in.
Create an art station with washable markers, stickers, and paper. Peeling and placing stickers is excellent fine motor practice.
Play with a ball: kick it, roll it, throw it. Your toddler is learning to coordinate whole-body movements with a moving target.
Your toddler is becoming a climber. Anchor all tall furniture, remove chairs near counters, and check for new climbing risks regularly.
Keep your toddler rear-facing in their car seat as long as they meet the seat's height and weight requirements. Rear-facing is safest.
Teach your toddler "hot" and "no touch" near the oven, stove, and fireplace. They are beginning to understand these warnings.
Never leave your toddler unattended in or near water, including toilets. Toddlers are top-heavy and can fall into a toilet headfirst.
Store all medications, vitamins, and supplements in child-proof containers in a locked cabinet. Toddlers can open more types of containers than you expect.
Cut food into pieces no larger than {{half an inch|1.5 cm}} for your toddler. Common choking hazards include whole grapes, hot dogs, raw carrots, and popcorn.
Use back burners when cooking and turn pot handles inward. Your toddler can now reach the front burners by pulling or climbing.
If you have a gun in the home, store it unloaded in a locked safe with ammunition locked separately. This is a critical safety measure recommended by pediatric experts.
Window falls are a serious risk at this age. Install window guards or stops that prevent windows from opening more than {{4 inches|10 cm}}.
Always supervise your toddler around pets, even gentle ones. Toddlers can inadvertently hurt animals, which may react defensively.
Practice saying your toddler's full name, your phone number, and address out loud to them. They won't remember it yet, but early exposure helps.
Check your home for laundry pods and dishwasher pods, which look like candy to toddlers. Store them in a high, locked cabinet.
Your toddler may learn to open doors. Install high deadbolts or doorknob covers on exterior doors to prevent unsupervised outdoor access.
Ensure your toddler wears a properly fitted life jacket near any open water, regardless of depth. Arm floaties are not a substitute.
Keep button batteries out of reach and secure battery compartments with screws. A swallowed button battery can cause serious internal burns within hours.
